articleTitle: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
summary: The review describes the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro as a faster laptop with more ports and a better display than the MacBook Air, but a $1,999 starting price and the MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021. It criticizes the absence of the flagship models’ OLED touchscreen and other design updates, particularly given the now-mandatory 1TB storage allotment and the $500 to $700 premium over MacBook Air alternatives.

coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The reviewer argues that a $1,999 entry-level MacBook Pro retains an older design and lacks the flagship OLED touchscreen and other updates, making its $500 to $700 premium over MacBook Air alternatives difficult to justify, especially for buyers who do not need the mandatory 1TB storage allotment.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: No regulatory precedent is stated. Historical comparisons include the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros retaining 2016-era designs and the Touch Bar, and the entry-level tier receiving the 2021-era design only with the M3 version released in 2023.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The $1,999 starting price does not include the optional $150 nano-texture matte display upgrade.
The 1TB storage allotment is now mandatory, including for buyers who do not need that capacity.
RAM options remain 16GB, 24GB, and 32GB; the reviewer identifies RAM as the biggest limitation for the kinds of models that run well on an M6.
The 16GB configuration is locked to 153 GB/s memory bandwidth, while the 24GB and 32GB configurations receive 170 GB/s.
The 16GB review unit has 90 percent of the memory bandwidth of the 24GB M6 Mac mini comparison unit, with slightly lower graphics/gaming results.
The entry-level model lacks a touchscreen, OLED panel, Dynamic Island, half-pound weight reduction, and glowing Apple logo despite its $1,999 starting price.
The M5 Pro's higher core count outperforms the M6 for multi-threaded CPU work, although the article credits the M6 with Apple's best single-core CPU performance and a larger Neural Engine.
The claim that M6 will not receive Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations is explicitly described as a rumor.
A future M6 MacBook Air is an expectation, not an announced release in the supplied text.
The reviewer's suggestion that an OLED touchscreen could take at least two years to reach this tier is speculation, not an Apple commitment.
Ongoing RAM and storage shortages are cited as complicating expectations for the product lineup's progression.
The article provides no exact release date, battery-life measurement, physical dimensions, camera resolution, numerical power consumption, or exact display pixel resolution.
No subscription requirement, cloud dependency, retention policy, or FCC approval status is discussed.

avoidAdvice: The review questions the value for buyers seeking Apple's best laptop display and newest design features: the $1,999 model lacks the flagship OLED touchscreen and other updates.
The review questions paying $500 to $700 more than a 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air, particularly when the mandatory 1TB storage allotment is unnecessary.
For M4 or M5 owners, the reviewer expects the M6 to feel faster but likely not staggeringly so.
fitAdvice: The model remains the cheapest Apple laptop option for a 120 Hz ProMotion display or the optional $150 anti-glare nano-texture finish.
Buyers prioritizing more built-in ports receive MagSafe, a pair of Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left and another on the right, a headphone jack, HDMI, and an SD card reader.
The reviewer says users upgrading from an M1 or M2 MacBook Air or Pro should notice a sizable improvement in day-to-day use.

For sustained workloads, the reviewer expects the actively cooled MacBook Pro to retain a performance advantage over a future fanless M6 MacBook Air; this comparison is prospective rather than a completed benchmark.
